overview: This entry covers Morocco from 1300 to 1492, chiefly the later Marinid era and the transition to Wattasid rule. Fez was a centre of government, learning and skilled production. The regional label spans political change rather than one uninterrupted dynasty.

periods.title: Later Marinid Morocco
periods.summary: Fez flourished under the Marinids, although royal authority weakened and powerful viziers competed for influence.

periods.title: From rebellion to Wattasid government
periods.summary: The last Marinid sultan died in the Fez rebellion of 1465; a Wattasid ruler secured Fez in 1472.

sections.title: A capital for rulers and students

items.text: The Marinids built Fez Jdid in 1276, before this entry’s first map year. It provided a new royal and military quarter beside the older city. A medieval capital could grow by adding a government town rather than by demolishing its existing neighbourhoods.

Marinid expansion reached Tunis in 1347, but the Black Death in 1348 and subsequent rebellions helped undermine this wider ambition. The dynasty’s cultural monuments outlasted its ability to hold a large North African empire together.

Buinaniya Madrasa in Fez was built in the 1350s. Its plan includes two facing classrooms and a prayer hall. A school building brought teaching, worship and the movement of students into one carefully arranged space.

Water crossed the madrasa’s southern side in a channel from the Wadi Lamtiyyin; two small bridges gave access to the prayer hall. A courtyard basin and an associated ablution building remind us that water supply and washing were practical parts of institutional life.

A hydraulic clock stood opposite Buinaniya. Water, architecture and the scheduling of communal life were connected here. The madrasa’s surviving fabric also includes later repairs, so a present-day view cannot be treated as an untouched photograph of the 1350s.

A Quran volume now in the Bavarian State Library was associated with the Marinid ruler Abu Yaqub Yusuf, who reigned from 1286 to 1307. It is the last part of a twelve-volume set, written on parchment in Maghribi script: a substantial book project rather than a pocket paperback.

A fourteenth-century door from a ruined Fez house survives in the Batha Museum. Its wood and wrought iron preserve a large main door with a smaller gate inside. Domestic craftsmanship deserves attention alongside the palace and mosque.

That door has two knockers of different sizes. The museum explains that the higher, larger one allowed a visitor riding a mule to knock without dismounting. Medieval convenience: the doorbell was adapted to the transport!

A ceiling fragment from the al-Misbahiya madrasa, built in 1346 to 1347, combines carved cedar pieces into stars and other geometric shapes. Traces of red, white, green and blue show that this wooden surface was once much more colourful than plain brown timber.

A tile panel from Buinaniya was made by removing parts of the glazed surface so that script stood out against the exposed background. The Batha fragment was recovered during modern restoration. It records both medieval craft and the later work of conserving it.

A silver half dirham struck at Azammur under Abd al-Haqq II names its ruler and mint. It weighs about 0.65 grams. Such a small object can locate an otherwise poorly documented mint within the political history of the fifteenth century.

The coin’s reverse includes امير المسلمين, “commander of the Muslims.” This Arabic title is shown in modern type from the published transcription. The coin belongs to Abd al-Haqq II’s reign, 1420 to 1465, rather than to every period labelled Morocco.

ending.text: The Marinid dynasty ended when Abd al-Haqq II was killed during the Fez rebellion of 1465. The Wattasids subsequently established their own government, securing Fez in 1472. Fez’s households, schools and workshops continued across the political transition, which falls inside this map entry’s dates.
